Praxis to provide production-like prompt corpus + traffic shape by 2027-07-22
Schedule 2-hour deep-dive perf run (synthetic replay) w/ Marcus + Diego the week of 2027-07-25
Redwood to share draft SLO matrix and measurement plan by 2027-07-23
action_items: Maya - send security docs + SOC2 summary - due 2027-07-20

transcript:
Header: 2027-07-18 16:00 PDT | Duration: ~48m
Attendees: Maya (Redwood AE), Diego (Redwood SE), Lena (CTO, Praxis), Marcus (Sr ML Eng), Aisha (Product)

Summary: Quick POC scoping to align on latency & throughput SLOs (TTFT vs TPOT), workload sizing, benchmark plan and timeline. Agreed to a 2-week pilot: week 1 baseline + synthetic replay; week 2 tuning and final SLO proposal.

Topics: TTFT definition and targets, TPOT definition (per-token latency / tokens-per-second), p95/p99 targets for interactive chat vs batch scoring, measurement methodology (replay vs synthetic), cache-warm vs cold, telemetry to collect.

[00:00] Maya: hey everyone thanks for joining, we're gonna keep this focused on the latency/throughput SLOs for the POC, probably 40ish minutes. quick intros?
[00:08] Lena: lena here, CTO at Praxis, we build a real-time insights engine for enterprise ops, our customers expect sub-second responses for short queries and streaming for longer chat flows.
[00:17] Marcus: marcus, I'll be running the benchmarks and hooking up the traffic replay. main constraints: we need predictable tail latency and cost under $X/token - but that cost piece we'll discuss later.
[00:27] Aisha: aisha, product, primarily interested in user perceived latency and what SLOs we can promise to customers.
[00:33] Diego: diego, Redwood SE, hi all. we'll propose measurement plan and sample goals and then adjust to Praxis' traffic.

[01:05] Maya: quick agenda: define TTFT vs TPOT so we're aligned, propose p95/p99 targets for interactive vs batch, agree on measurement plan + tooling, and timeline. sound good?
[01:15] Lena: yes.

[02:10] Diego: ok so definitions — TTFT we use as Time To First Token: from request arrival at gateway to first byte of model output. that maps to perceived latency for interactive customers. TPOT — we've been using it internally as Time Per Output Token (inverse of tokens/sec). so when we say TPOT p95 40ms that's ~25 tokens/sec. important distinction: TTFT covers initial overhead (routing, model load, kv cache recovery), TPOT is steady-state generation cost.
[02:45] Marcus: is TPOT normally reported as ms/token or tokens/sec? our analytics dashboard expects tokens/sec.
[02:51] Diego: totally, both are fine; we'll report ms/token and tokens/sec. ms/token is easier for tail-latency math.

[04:05] Lena: give us an example target for a chat path: real-time chat for support agents, prompts ~40-120 tokens, response maybe 60 tokens. what would you target?
[04:18] Diego: for interactive chat we typically propose TTFT p95 <= 300ms, p99 <= 600-700ms; TPOT p95 <= 45ms/token (so roughly 22 tokens/sec), TPOT p99 <= 90-120ms/token for the worst tail. those are starting points and depend on model size and quantization.
[04:42] Marcus: that p99 700ms seems high for TTFT — our SLA goal is to promise sub-500ms almost always for agent UI. can you get lower?
[04:53] Diego: yes on dedicated infra and aggressive warm KV cache we can push TTFT p95 to 200-250ms. hosted noisy neighbors or cold starts will push tails higher. it's a tradeoff: cost vs tail.

[06:10] Aisha: for longer generation (like summarization 300-500 tokens) user cares less about TTFT and more about throughput/cost. what should we measure there?
[06:20] Maya: right, for larger jobs measure aggregated time to finish (TTOT?) and average TPOT; we capture both token rate and end-to-end completion time. for batch use cases we usually set p95 completion time target and an overall throughput target (requests/sec or tokens/sec per cluster).

[07:05] Marcus: ok so concrete success criteria for POC: we want to validate we can meet TTFT p95 <= 250ms for chat with 95% fidelity on our prompt set, and steady-state TPOT p95 <= 50ms/token. if you can show that on dedicated or hosted with clear cost numbers, we can move forward.
[07:27] Diego: makes sense. we'll aim to demonstrate both model variants: quantized vv float; also show routing fallback to smaller variant if tails spike.

[08:10] Maya: measurement plan — here's how we run it:
- week 1 day 1: baseline single-request latency on sample prompts (cold/warm cache separated)
- day 2: synthetic load tests with Locust (we'll share scripts) to exercise concurrency patterns you see in production (we need shape from Marcus)
- day 3: traffic replay using your anonymized logs to validate realistic tails
- day 4: cost/throughput analysis and SLO proposal

[08:41] Marcus: we can produce 48h of logs and a sample corpus by Friday. the traffic shape is spiky — 10x peaks during business hours, about 60% short chat, 40% long jobs.
[08:55] Diego: perfect, that's the mix we need. note: replay tests measure realistic prefix caching benefits — you should get much better TPOT in replay vs synthetic cold runs.

[10:00] Lena: how do you handle cache warm vs cold in reporting? we need to be clear because our users will measure perceived latency from first tenant traffic.
[10:08] Diego: we'll report three curves: cold start (empty model cache), warm steady-state with KV/prefix cache primed, and production-like replay (includes warmed cache plus network variability). SLOs will specify which curve they apply to — e.g., TTFT SLO applies to warm steady-state.

[11:30] Aisha: instrumentation — what telemetry do we need to collect from our side?
[11:40] Diego: request timestamps (ingest), first-byte sent, last-byte sent, token counts, model variant, host/gpu id. also we ask for a small set of logs with request ids so we can correlate with console traces. Redwood Console will ingest traces and show token-level breakdowns.

[12:50] Marcus: will you include GPU metrics? p99 queue times?
[12:55] Diego: yes we collect GPU utilization, queue depth, per-request kernel time (where available), and KV cache hit rates. we'll include tail queue times in the report.

[14:10] Maya: benchmarks: we'll run both open model variants you plan to use plus a Redwood-verified baseline (we'll include a smaller model to show fallbacks). We'll provide a report with p50/p95/p99 for TTFT and TPOT, plus throughput numbers (max sustainable requests/sec at target SLO).

[15:02] Marcus: how do you compute sustainable throughput? we need guidance so engineering can capacity plan.
[15:09] Diego: we ramp concurrent requests until we see SLO breaches at target percentile, and then back-off to a safety margin (e.g., 80% of the breach point). That yields a recommended RPS for that model/config. We'll also show batch and batching impacts.

[16:20] Lena: and for cost modeling?
[16:26] Maya: we'll compute cost-per-1M tokens and cost-per-request at your average prompt/response length for each config. that lets you compare hosted vs dedicated.

[17:15] Marcus: curious about measuring TTFT vs TPOT on streaming responses — our UI streams tokens as they arrive.
[17:24] Diego: for streaming we measure initial TTFT to first token and then tokens/sec during streaming; we'll capture the inter-token jitter (ms between tokens) and include p95/p99 of that too. jitter matters for perceived smoothness.

[19:01] Aisha: what about user-level SLAs where they care about a probabilistic metric like "95% of sessions see average latency < 500ms"?
[19:10] Diego: we can map request-level p95/p99 to session-level guarantees by sampling sessions and aggregating. we'll provide recommended session metrics and how to compute them from request logs.

[20:05] Marcus: tooling — you mentioned locust. any specifics on the script or artifacts you will share?
[20:12] Diego: yes we'll share a locust script with parameterized prompt lengths, concurrency, and rate shapes. we also have a replay tool that consumes anonymized logs and replays exact timestamps to the Redwood test cluster. script and runbook will be in the repo link we send.

[22:00] Lena: timeline — we'd like results within 2 weeks. is that doable?
[22:07] Maya: yes two-week pilot: week 1 baseline & synthetic + replay, week 2 tuning and final SLOs + cost analysis. deliverable: raw results, SLO matrix (TTFT/TPOT p50/p95/p99), recommended capacity and cost estimates, and short slides.

[23:11] Marcus: what about noise from multi-tenant hosted? if you show hosted numbers, will you also show dedicated?
[23:19] Diego: we will. hosted for quick evaluation, and one dedicated run to show the delta. dedicated usually reduces variance and tails; we'll quantify the improvement.

[25:05] Maya: failure modes to test: region failover, fallback to smaller model, and degrade-to-summary mode. we'll simulate model failures and ensure graceful degradation. We'll include automatic fallback policy testing in the run.

[27:00] Aisha: security/compliance ask — we need KMS integration and audit logs for production.
[27:08] Maya: noted. I'll include the SOC2/KMS integration docs in the email.

[28:40] Marcus: sample SLO matrix (proposal):
- Interactive chat (short prompts ~60 tokens): TTFT p95 <= 250ms, TTFT p99 <= 600ms; TPOT p95 <= 50ms/token, TPOT p99 <= 110ms/token.
- Long generation (300-500 tokens): Completion time p95 <= 6s, TPOT avg <= 45ms/token; throughput target: sustain 10 concurrent long jobs w/o SLO breaches.
- Batch scoring: throughput goal 200 req/s for 2k prompt length within cost X.

[30:05] Diego: those look reasonable as targets; we'll validate and adjust. we'll also show what changes if you enable quantization and batching.

[31:20] Lena: what about variance across regions? we plan to run in us-west and eu-west.
[31:27] Diego: we'll run baseline in both regions if you want — that adds a day to the schedule but we can highlight region delta.

[33:15] Marcus: sample size for p99 estimates?
[33:20] Diego: to get stable p99 you need >10k requests per test window; we'll run each scenario for sufficient duration and aggregate windows. we'll provide bootstrap confidence intervals for p99.

[35:00] Aisha: any gotchas?
[35:05] Diego: yes — make sure replay logs keep original timestamps and avoid client-side timestamps that jitter; prime your prefix cache if you want to emulate warm state; and watch out for tokenization differences between models which change token counts and therefore cost/TPOT.

[36:40] Marcus: for the traffic shape we have spikes up to 10k rps — can Redwood simulate that?
[36:47] Diego: we can run scaled synthetic tests in our testbed but for absolute scale we'll coordinate on dedicated infra or run in your cloud account with our scripts. we'll document the recommended cluster size to meet your peak.

[38:00] Maya: recap / next steps: Marcus provides logs and corpus, Redwood shares locust/replay scripts and runs week 1 baseline, we present results and SLO proposal week 2. security docs + SOC2 summary delivered by Maya. schedule deep-dive run with Marcus & Diego.

[38:25] Lena: agreed. thanks everyone.

[38:30] Marcus: thanks.

[38:33] Aisha: thanks!

[39:00] (small side chatter about calendar invites and links)

[43:55] Maya: I'll follow up in email with links, runbook and timeline. Expect draft SLO matrix by 2027-07-23.

[44:10] Diego: I'll attach the locust script and the replay tool link.

[44:20] Meeting ended.

Notes / artifacts referenced: redwood runbook link (shared), locust script (shared), replay tool (shared), sample SLO matrix (to be drafted).

End of transcript.
